pages.text: The road to Abha twisted up into the mountains like a grey ribbon. Hamad pressed his face against the car window as clouds drifted below them. "We're actually higher than the clouds!" he said. His cousin Yousef laughed, but Uncle Saleh reminded them that mountains could change their mood very quickly.

Early the next morning, the three of them set off along a narrow trail toward a hidden waterfall. Juniper trees grew between the rocks, and baboons watched them from a cliff. Uncle Saleh gave each boy a whistle and a bottle of water. "If you ever get lost, stay calm and blow the whistle three times," he explained.

After two hours, they finally heard the roar of falling water. As Uncle Saleh stepped onto a wet rock to take a photo, his foot slipped. He fell awkwardly and cried out in pain. "I think I've twisted my ankle badly," he said, his face pale.

Yousef checked his phone, but there was no signal at all. Then, without warning, thick fog began to roll down the mountain, hiding the path in white. Hamad felt his heart beating fast. "We can't carry you, Uncle," he said. "What should we do?"

Uncle Saleh thought for a moment. "There's a farm at the bottom of the valley," he said. "Follow the stream downhill and look for the red marks painted on the rocks. Stay together, and don't take any risks."

The boys moved carefully through the fog, which was so dense they could barely see ten metres ahead. Twice they lost the trail, but each time Yousef spotted another faded red mark. When the stream disappeared beneath some huge boulders, Hamad almost panicked. Then he remembered the whistle and blew three long blasts.

From somewhere below, a dog barked, and a man's voice called back. Soon an elderly shepherd appeared out of the mist with his dog beside him. "Assalamu alaikum, boys! What are you doing up here in this weather?" he asked kindly. The boys quickly explained everything.

The shepherd, Abu Nasser, phoned for help from his farm, and two rescuers soon reached Uncle Saleh with a stretcher. That evening, the whole family gathered around Uncle Saleh, whose ankle was wrapped in a bandage. "You two were brave and sensible," he said proudly. Hamad smiled, but he secretly decided that next time he would check the weather forecast first.

options: Never go to the mountains again

stories.title: The Night of the Little Turtles

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal and his younger sister Noura stayed with their uncle Khalid in a small town on the Red Sea coast. Uncle Khalid worked for a marine protection centre, and he knew more about sea animals than anyone Faisal had ever met. On their first evening, he showed them a part of the beach that was surrounded by a low rope fence. "A green turtle laid her eggs here two months ago," he explained. "They could hatch any night now, so we must keep this place safe."

Faisal had read that baby turtles find the sea by following the light of the moon on the water. "So they don't need any help?" he asked. "Usually not," said his uncle. "But only about one in a thousand baby turtles survives to become an adult, so every single one matters." Noura promised she would check the nest every day, and Faisal decided he would too.

A few days later, Uncle Khalid had to drive to Jeddah for an important meeting. "I'll be back tomorrow afternoon," he told them. "Your aunt Maha is here if you need anything." That evening, Faisal noticed something worrying. Workers had put up bright new lights at a café that was being built near the road, just behind the beach.

After dinner, Faisal and Noura walked down to the nest with a torch, as they had done every night. At first, everything seemed quiet. Then Noura grabbed his arm. "Look! The sand is moving!" Tiny dark shapes were pushing their way out of the ground, one after another, until there were dozens of them.

But instead of heading towards the dark sea, the little turtles were crawling the wrong way, straight towards the bright café lights and the road. Faisal's heart was beating fast. "They think the lights are the moon!" he cried. "If they reach the road, the cars will hit them." He knew they had no time to lose.

Faisal tried to phone his uncle, but there was no answer. "Noura, run home and get Aunt Maha," he said. "Ask her to call the café owner and tell him to turn off those lights!" While his sister raced back to the house, Faisal switched off his torch and lay down on the sand between the turtles and the road, using his body as a wall. Gently, he began to turn the turtles around with his hands, one by one.

Ten long minutes passed. Then, suddenly, the café lights went out, and the beach became dark except for the silver moonlight on the waves. Almost immediately, the turtles changed direction. Faisal watched in amazement as dozens of tiny turtles hurried across the wet sand and disappeared into the sea.

When Uncle Khalid came home the next day, he listened to the whole story without saying a word. Then he smiled proudly. "You both kept your heads and saved almost the whole nest," he said. "I've already spoken to the café owner, and he has agreed to use special turtle-safe lights from now on." That night, Faisal stood on the quiet beach and looked out at the dark water, wondering how many of his little turtles would one day return to this same beach to lay their own eggs.

pages.text: Layla had been waiting for this night for three weeks. Her school was holding a competition, and the challenge was simple but difficult: take a clear photograph of the International Space Station as it crossed the sky. Her grandfather had driven her and her little brother, Faris, far into the desert near AlUla, where there were no city lights to hide the stars. "The station will pass over us at exactly 9:14," Layla announced, checking her tablet for the tenth time.

While Faris helped their grandfather make sweet tea over a small fire, Layla set up her camera on its stand. The app on her tablet showed a bright line across a map of the sky, marking the station's path. "It moves at almost 28,000 kilometres an hour," she told Faris. "If I point the camera in the wrong direction, I'll miss it completely." Faris looked up at the endless stars and whistled quietly.

At five minutes to nine, the screen of her tablet suddenly went black. Layla pressed the button again and again, but nothing happened, because she had forgotten to charge it before they left. Her heart sank. Without the map, how would she know where to look in such an enormous sky?

Her grandfather put down his cup and sat beside her on the cool sand. "Long before there were screens, our grandparents crossed this desert at night using only the stars," he said calmly. "Tell me what you remember about the path." Layla closed her eyes and tried to picture the map. "It rises in the northwest," she said slowly, "and then it passes very close to a bright star called Vega."

Her grandfather smiled and pointed to a brilliant blue-white light high above them. "That is Vega," he said. "Its name comes from Arabic, an-nasr al-waqi, which means 'the falling eagle.' Astronomers all over the world still use hundreds of star names that were given by Arab scientists centuries ago." Layla stared at the star, amazed that she had never known this before.

At 9:14, a steady point of light appeared low in the northwest. "Is that a plane?" Faris shouted, jumping up. "No," their grandfather replied. "Planes have flashing lights, but the station shines without blinking, because it reflects sunlight." With shaking hands, Layla turned her camera towards the falling eagle and waited.

The light climbed higher and higher, moving silently and smoothly across the darkness. Just as it reached Vega, Layla pressed the button and kept the camera open for several seconds. When she checked the picture, she gasped. A long, bright line ran across the sky, passing right beside the star, as if the eagle were racing the station.

Two weeks later, Layla's photograph won first prize, and her teacher hung it in the school's main hall. Under the picture, Layla had written its title: "The Eagle and the Station." That evening, she gave a framed copy to her grandfather, who said she should keep learning the names of the stars, so she would never feel lost again. Layla promised she would, and she also promised something else: from now on, she would always charge her tablet.

pages.text: Yousef had been the top scorer at Al-Noor School for two seasons, and everyone expected him to lead the team in the city final. Then, ten days before the match, he landed badly during training and felt a sharp pain in his ankle. The doctor looked at the X-ray and shook his head. "Three weeks of rest," he said. "No running, no football."

Yousef spent the next few days feeling sorry for himself. He refused to watch his teammates practise because it was too painful to sit and do nothing. His grandfather, who had played for a local club when he was young, found him staring at the wall one evening. "You think a player is only useful when he's kicking the ball?" he asked. "The best players I knew watched more than they ran."

The next afternoon, Yousef limped to the training ground with crutches and a small notebook. Coach Hamad raised his eyebrows but said nothing as Yousef sat down on the bench. While the others trained, Yousef wrote down everything he noticed: who got tired first, who always passed to the right, and who panicked under pressure. By the end of the week, the notebook was half full.

On Thursday, Coach Hamad showed the team a video of their opponents, Al-Faris Academy, who hadn't lost a match all year. Yousef asked to watch it again, and then a third time. "Their goalkeeper is excellent," he said slowly, "but look: before every penalty, he touches his left glove, and then he dives to his left." The coach paused the video, rewound it, and a smile spread across his face. "Well spotted, but keep that to yourself until Saturday," he said.

The final was held at the city stadium, and the stands were packed with families waving green and white flags. Al-Faris scored early, and for most of the first half Al-Noor couldn't get near the ball. At half-time, Yousef pointed out that their number seven always slowed down when he had to use his left foot. Coach Hamad changed the plan, and fifteen minutes later Khalid stole the ball from number seven and scored the equaliser.

Neither team managed another goal, so the match went to penalties. The stadium fell silent as the players walked to the centre circle. Coach Hamad gathered his team and nodded towards Yousef. "Whoever takes a penalty, listen carefully," Yousef said. "Watch his left glove, and then shoot to the right."

One by one, the Al-Noor players stepped up, and one by one the goalkeeper touched his glove and dived the wrong way. When Al-Faris missed their fourth kick, it was all down to Khalid. His hands were shaking, but he glanced at the bench, and Yousef gave him a thumbs-up. Khalid ran forward and placed the ball calmly into the right corner of the net.

The players went wild, but instead of running to the crowd, they ran straight to the bench and lifted Yousef, crutches and all, onto their shoulders. When the captain received the trophy, he handed it to Yousef first. That evening, Yousef's grandfather held the medal up to the light and laughed. "So," he said, "who really won the match today?" Yousef smiled, tapped his notebook and said, "I think I helped, without touching the ball once."

options: Goalkeepers are the most important players.

It is better to watch football than to play it.

stories.title: The Thief in the Palm Tree

pages.text: Every winter, Lama and her older brother Yousef spent a week at their grandfather's farm near AlUla, surrounded by palm trees and red rocks. This year, however, something strange had been happening there. "Things keep disappearing," Grandfather told them over a cup of Arabic coffee. "First my car keys, then a silver spoon, and yesterday the shiny buttons from my old jacket."

Yousef put down his cup. "Has anyone new come to the farm recently?" he asked. Grandfather mentioned Saeed, a young man who had started helping with the date harvest a month earlier. Later, Yousef whispered to his sister, "It must be him, because the thefts began when he arrived." Lama frowned, as she didn't like jumping to conclusions without any evidence.

The next morning brought the biggest shock of all: Grandfather's old brass dallah, which had once belonged to his own father, was missing from the majlis. Yousef was now completely sure who the thief was. Lama, however, noticed that the window had been left open, and she found a small black feather on the carpet. She also realised that nothing valuable, like money, had ever been taken, only things that shone.

Determined to discover the truth, Lama decided to keep an eye on that window. She sat quietly behind the curtain all afternoon with her notebook on her knees. Just before sunset, a large grey-and-black crow landed on the windowsill. It hopped inside, picked up Grandmother's reading glasses from the table and flew straight towards the tallest palm tree.

Lama ran to tell Yousef and Grandfather, and Saeed quickly brought a long ladder. He climbed carefully to the top of the tree. "You won't believe this!" he shouted. Inside the nest were the keys, the spoon, the buttons, the glasses, some bottle caps and a small gold ring. Grandmother gasped, because it was the wedding ring she had lost fifteen years before.

But the dallah wasn't in the nest. "A crow could never carry something that heavy," Lama pointed out. Yousef looked at Saeed uncomfortably, but Saeed just smiled. "Oh, the dallah? I took it to a shop in town this morning, because your grandfather asked me to have it polished and repaired before Friday's family dinner." Grandfather laughed and hit his forehead. "Of course! I completely forgot that I had asked you!"

Yousef's face turned red with embarrassment. He apologised to Saeed and admitted that he had suspected him without any proof. "Don't worry, no harm done," Saeed replied kindly. Lama gave her brother a meaningful look. "Real detectives follow the evidence, not their guesses," she said.

On Friday evening the whole family gathered in the majlis, where the dallah shone like new and Grandmother proudly wore her ring again. Grandfather raised his cup towards Lama and called her the cleverest detective in AlUla. Outside, the crow watched them from the top of its palm tree, perhaps searching for its next treasure. Laughing, Yousef quickly took off his shiny watch and hid it in his pocket.

pages.text: Every night at nine o'clock, a small light flashed from a seventh-floor window in Jeddah. Across the street, Hamza was always waiting with his own torch in his hand. He and his best friend Tariq had learned Morse code from an old book two summers ago, and since then they had sent each other a secret message every single night. Short flash, long flash, short flash: it was a language that only the two of them understood.

Then came the school football final. In the last minute, Hamza missed an easy goal, and their team lost. While everyone else was silent, Tariq laughed loudly and shouted, "My grandmother could have scored that!" The whole team heard it, and Hamza's face burned with embarrassment.

That night, Hamza didn't pick up his torch. When Tariq's light flashed "ARE YOU THERE?", he closed his curtains and turned his back on the window. At school the next day, he gave Tariq the cold shoulder and sat with other boys at break. A whole week passed, and the window across the street stayed dark.

On Thursday evening, a terrible storm hit the city. Strong winds shook the palm trees, and suddenly every light in the neighbourhood went out. Hamza's mother lit candles, and his father went to check on the neighbours. Hamza was staring into the darkness from his window when he noticed something strange.

A tiny light was flashing from the seventh floor: three short, three long, three short. Hamza's heart began to race. He had seen this pattern in the book many times. It was S-O-S, the signal for help, and Tariq would never joke about that, not even after a week of silence.

Hamza grabbed his torch, shouted for his father and ran across the wet street. The lift wasn't working, so they climbed seven floors of stairs in the dark. Tariq opened the door, and his face was pale. "It's my grandmother," he said. "She fell, my phone is dead, and my parents are stuck at my uncle's house because of the storm."

Hamza's father knelt beside the old woman and checked her ankle carefully. "It's badly twisted, but I don't think it's broken," he said calmly, and he used his own phone to call Tariq's parents. Later, Tariq said quietly, "I'm really sorry about the match. I thought I was being funny, but I was just being unkind." Hamza grinned and replied, "You can make it up to me by teaching your grandmother to play football."

Even with her painful ankle, Tariq's grandmother laughed louder than both of them. When the electricity came back an hour later, the two boys stood at their windows again. Slowly, Tariq's light spelled out a question across the street: FRIENDS? Hamza didn't need the old book to answer, and with a big smile he flashed back one word: ALWAYS.

stories.title: The Stone That Fell from the Stars

pages.text: Omar had always thought the desert at night was completely silent. But on the last evening of their camping trip, as he sat by the fire with his grandfather and his cousin Yousef, the sky suddenly lit up. A ball of green fire raced across the stars, leaving a long, glowing tail behind it. A few seconds later, they heard a low boom, like distant thunder.

"Was that a plane?" Yousef whispered. Grandfather shook his head slowly. "I have lived in this desert for seventy years, and I have only seen something like that twice. It was a meteor, a rock from space." Omar's heart was beating fast. "If part of it reached the ground, it could be somewhere near here!"

The next morning, while Grandfather made tea, Omar found one bar of phone signal and started reading. He learned that most meteorites are dark, surprisingly heavy, and often contain iron. Their surface usually has a thin black crust, which forms when the rock burns as it falls through the atmosphere. "Finding one out here is like looking for a needle in a haystack," Yousef said. "Then we need a smarter plan than just walking around," Omar replied.

Grandfather took a strong magnet from an old car speaker and tied it to the end of his walking stick. Using the direction of the fiery tail and the sound of the boom, the boys chose an area to the north of the camp. For hours, they walked slowly in straight lines, sweeping the magnet over the sand. By noon, the sun was burning, their shoes were full of sand, and Yousef was ready to give up.

Then, with a sharp click, something jumped onto the magnet. It was a black stone about the size of an egg, and its surface looked like chocolate that had melted and hardened again. Omar wanted to grab it, but he remembered what he had read: oil from human skin can damage a meteorite. Carefully, he wrapped it in clean foil from their lunch and saved the exact location on his phone.

Back in Riyadh, Grandfather contacted Dr. Hassan, a geology professor at the university. He cut a tiny corner off the stone and examined it under a microscope while the boys held their breath. Inside, there were shiny flakes of metal and hundreds of tiny round grains. "These grains are called chondrules," Dr. Hassan explained, "and they were formed about four and a half billion years ago, before the Earth even existed."

The stone was a real meteorite, and Omar's careful notes turned out to be extremely useful. Using the location he had saved, a team of scientists returned to the desert and discovered twelve more pieces. Dr. Hassan explained that meteorites are always named after the nearest place where they are found. From then on, it would be known around the world as the "Bir Al-Ghaf meteorite," after the old well near their camp.

Dr. Hassan told Omar he could keep his stone, but Omar decided to give it to the university museum so that students could study it for years to come. To thank him, the professor gave him a thin, polished slice in a small glass case. "For seventy years I have watched the sky," Grandfather said proudly, "but it was my grandsons who caught a piece of it." That night, Omar looked up at the stars and realised that every single one was hiding a question waiting to be answered.

pages.text: Every winter, Faris's family drove deep into the desert to camp for a weekend, far from the noise of Riyadh. This year, Faris had brought something new: a small drone with a camera, a birthday present he had been dreaming about for months. "I'm going to film the dunes from the sky," he told his grandmother, Noura, as she poured cardamom coffee by the fire. She smiled and said, "The desert has its own ideas, habibi. Make sure you listen to it."

That evening, she told them a story she had heard from her father. Long ago, when he travelled with camels, he had found a hidden well between three dunes shaped like a sleeping camel. "The sand swallowed it years later," she said quietly, "and nobody has seen it since." Faris's older sister, Lama, rolled her eyes, but Faris couldn't stop thinking about it.

The next morning, Faris launched the drone while his father was checking the car's tyres. At first everything went perfectly, and the screen showed golden waves of sand stretching to the horizon. Then a sudden gust caught the drone and pushed it beyond the tallest dune. The screen froze, and a warning appeared: "Signal lost."

"It can't have gone far," Faris said, his heart sinking. Lama sighed and picked up two bottles of water. "I'm coming with you, but we tell Dad first and we come straight back." Their father agreed on one condition: they had to stay where they could see the tall flag above the tents.

They climbed the dune, their feet sliding in the soft sand, and found the drone lying on the other side. Faris was so relieved that he didn't notice the sky turning a strange orange colour. Then Lama pointed. A brown wall of dust was rolling towards them, and the flag had already disappeared behind it.

Faris remembered his grandmother's words: "When the sand flies, don't run. Sit low, cover your face and wait." They crouched against the side of the dune that faced away from the wind and pulled their scarves over their mouths. The wind howled for what felt like hours, although it was only twenty minutes. Lama held his hand tightly, and for once, she didn't tease him.

When the dust finally settled, everything looked different, but Faris noticed the small ripples in the sand. "Grandma says the ripples show us where the wind came from," he said, "and the storm came from the direction of the camp." They walked carefully, following the pattern, until they heard their father calling their names. He hugged them both so hard that Faris could hardly breathe.

That night, Faris watched the drone's last recording with his whole family. Just before it fell, the camera had caught three curved dunes like a sleeping camel, and between them, a ring of old stones, half-buried in the sand. Grandma Noura stared at the screen with tears in her eyes. "My father's well," she whispered. "The desert kept it safe all these years, and now it has shown it to you, because you listened."

pages.text: Yousef had spent three weeks building his invention for the school Innovation Day. It was a small round robot that cleaned floors, and he had added a camera so it could recognise and follow one person. "It's called Shadow," he told his best friend Khalid proudly. "Just show it a face, and it will follow that person anywhere, cleaning the floor behind them." Khalid looked doubtful. "What could possibly go wrong?" he said.

On the morning of Innovation Day, the hall was full of parents, teachers and nervous students. Yousef planned to show Shadow his own face. But just as he pressed the button, the head teacher, Mr. Al-Harbi, leaned over the table to say good morning. Shadow's little light turned green, it beeped twice, and then it began to roll after Mr. Al-Harbi as he walked away.

At first, nobody noticed. Mr. Al-Harbi shook hands with an important visitor from the Ministry of Education, and Shadow waited politely behind his shoes. When he walked to the volcano project, Shadow followed. When he stopped to try the dates at the snack table, Shadow stopped too, and quietly vacuumed up every crumb he dropped.

"Yousef," Khalid whispered, "your robot has a new best friend." Yousef's face went red. He grabbed the remote control and pressed STOP, but nothing happened, because the batteries had fallen out somewhere under the table. "If he finds out, I'm finished," Yousef groaned, crawling on the floor to look for them.

Then Mr. Al-Harbi turned around suddenly and almost stepped on Shadow. He jumped to the left, and Shadow went left. He moved to the right, and Shadow went right. The whole hall went silent, and then a small boy in the front row started to laugh. Soon everyone was laughing, including the visitor from the Ministry, who was wiping tears from his eyes.

Yousef finally found the batteries, but it was too late to hide. He walked to the front of the hall with his heart beating fast. "I'm really sorry, sir," he said. "It was supposed to follow me, not you." Mr. Al-Harbi looked down at the little robot, which was waiting patiently by his feet like a loyal cat.

For a long moment, the head teacher said nothing. Then he smiled. "In twenty years of teaching," he said, "this is the first time a student has helped me keep the floor clean." The visitor asked Yousef how the camera worked, and Yousef explained everything, forgetting to be nervous. By the end, a crowd had gathered around them, asking questions.

Yousef didn't win first prize, because that went to a boy who had built a solar-powered water cooler. But he got a special award for "Most Loyal Invention," and Mr. Al-Harbi asked if Shadow could stay in his office for a week. "Of course, sir," said Yousef with a grin. For the next seven days, every student knew exactly when the head teacher was coming. They just listened for the beep.

pages.text: Every summer, Faisal stayed with his grandfather on the Farasan Islands in the Red Sea. Grandfather had been a fisherman for forty years, and he knew the sea like the back of his hand. Each morning, before the sun became too hot, they walked together along the empty beach. Faisal loved these walks, because the waves always left something interesting on the sand.

One morning, Faisal noticed a dark shape near the rocks. As they came closer, he realised it was a large sea turtle, trapped in an old green fishing net. The turtle was hardly moving, and one of her flippers was badly tangled. "Quick, let's pull it off!" Faisal shouted. "Wait," said Grandfather calmly. "If we pull too hard, the net will cut her. We have to be patient."

Grandfather took out his small knife and began cutting the net, one piece at a time. While he worked, Faisal kept the turtle's head wet with sea water from his bottle. When the last piece fell away, Faisal noticed a small metal tag on one of her flippers. It had a number, 214, and a phone number printed underneath. "Someone has been looking after this turtle before us," Grandfather said with a smile.

Faisal called the number immediately, and a woman answered. Her name was Dr. Nora, and she was a marine scientist who studied turtles in the Red Sea. "Number 214? I know her well!" she said excitedly. "Please keep her in the shade. I'll be there by boat within an hour." While they waited, Faisal couldn't stop wondering where the turtle had travelled since she was tagged.

When Dr. Nora arrived, she examined the turtle carefully and then looked up, surprised. "She's carrying eggs," she explained. "Turtles return to the same beach where they were born, sometimes after swimming thousands of kilometres. She was coming home when the net caught her." She also told them that lost fishing nets are called ghost nets, because they keep catching sea animals for years, even when nobody is using them.

By sunset, the turtle was strong enough to go back into the water. Faisal watched her slowly crawl across the sand until the waves covered her shell, and then she was gone. "I'll never see her again," he said sadly. Grandfather put a hand on his shoulder. "Don't be so sure," he said. "The sea has a way of keeping its promises."

Two weeks later, Faisal's phone rang late in the evening. "There are fresh tracks on your beach," Dr. Nora whispered. Faisal and his grandfather hurried outside, using only a red torch so they wouldn't frighten anything. There, in the moonlight, was turtle 214, digging a deep hole with her back flippers. They sat silently and watched as she laid more than a hundred white eggs.

For the rest of the summer, Faisal and his friends collected ghost nets from the rocks, and Dr. Nora taught them how to protect the nest. Then, one warm night near the end of August, the sand began to move. Dozens of tiny turtles climbed out and raced bravely towards the silver waves. "You were right, Grandfather," Faisal said quietly. "The sea kept its promise, and now I'm going to keep mine."

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef spent a week at his grandfather's farm in Al-Ahsa, where hundreds of date palms stood in long green rows. This year, though, something was wrong. Some of the leaves had turned brown, and his grandfather, Abu Saleh, looked tired and worried. "Water is getting more expensive," he explained, "and I can't tell which trees really need it, so I water them all."

That night, Yousef couldn't sleep. He had recently read an article about sensors that measure how wet the soil is, and an idea started to grow in his mind. What if each palm could tell his grandfather when it was thirsty? By sunrise, he had filled three pages of his notebook with drawings and arrows.

Back in Riyadh, he collected old phones, broken toys and wires from his uncle's repair shop. His older sister Noura, who was studying engineering, helped him understand circuits, although she laughed when he burned his finger for the second time. After four weeks, he had a prototype: a small box with two metal sticks that went into the soil. When the soil became too dry, the box played a recording of his grandfather's voice saying, "I'm thirsty! Bring me water!"

His science teacher, Mr. Khalid, was impressed and suggested entering the national young inventors' competition. "Your idea is simple, cheap and useful," he said. "Those are exactly the three things judges look for." So Yousef worked every evening after his homework, testing the box in the family garden until the neighbours' cat ran away every time it spoke.

On the day of the competition, the hall was full of amazing inventions, from robot arms to smart glasses. When it was Yousef's turn, he pushed the metal sticks into a pot of dry sand and waited proudly. Nothing happened. His face went hot as the judges wrote their notes, and someone at the back laughed quietly.

Afterwards, Noura opened the box and found the problem immediately: a tiny wire had melted because he had left the box in the hot car. "So it isn't a bad idea," she said gently. "It just needs a better design." Yousef didn't win a prize, but one of the judges, an engineer called Dr. Huda, gave him her card and said, "Every inventor fails on stage at least once. Call me when it works."

All autumn, Yousef improved his invention. He added a small solar panel so the battery would never run out, and he covered the wires with heat-resistant material so the Al-Ahsa sun couldn't damage them. In the winter holiday, he and his grandfather placed twenty boxes beside twenty palms. Soon the farm was full of Abu Saleh's own voice calling "I'm thirsty!" from different corners, and he laughed so hard that he had to sit down.

By the next summer, the farm was using almost half as much water, and the brown leaves had turned green again. Yousef sent Dr. Huda a video, and two weeks later she invited him to present his boxes at her university. Before he left, his grandfather put a hand on his shoulder. "In the competition, your box was silent," he said, "but here, it has been talking all year. That is the prize that really matters."

pages.text: Faisal had been looking forward to this trip for months. His father had a work meeting in Kuala Lumpur, and this time Faisal was allowed to come too. Before they left Riyadh, his mother tied a bright yellow ribbon to his suitcase. "So you can find it easily," she said, but Faisal quietly took it off and pushed it into his backpack. He was thirteen, after all, and ribbons were for little kids.

After a long night flight, they waited by the baggage belt in the busy airport. Dozens of suitcases went round and round, and many of them looked exactly the same. When Faisal saw a dark blue one with a broken wheel, he grabbed it at once. "That's mine," he said confidently, and they hurried outside to catch a taxi to the hotel.

That evening, Faisal opened the suitcase to get his phone charger, and his heart sank. Instead of his clothes, he found brown shoes, neatly folded shirts and a small wooden box. Inside the box was an old brass compass with words carved on the back: "For Amir, so you never lose your way." "Dad," Faisal called nervously, "I think I've made a big mistake."

His father looked through the suitcase carefully, searching for a name or an address. In a side pocket, he found a crumpled boarding pass from their flight and a card from a small guesthouse in the old part of the city. "If the owner is staying there, he must be worried sick," his father said. Faisal felt terrible, especially when he thought about the compass. It was clearly a present, and someone had chosen it with love.

Early the next morning, they took the train across the city and walked through narrow streets full of food stalls and colourful shops. The guesthouse was tiny, with green plants hanging above the door. Behind the desk sat an elderly man with a grey beard, and next to him was Faisal's own blue suitcase! "You must be the boy who loves football magazines," the man said with a smile.

The man introduced himself as Mr. Hamid. He was Malaysian, but he had spent a month in Riyadh visiting his daughter, and now he was home again to see his grandson, Amir. "I didn't sleep at all last night," he admitted. "I was going to give Amir that compass at dinner tonight. It belonged to my own father."

Faisal apologised again and again, but Mr. Hamid just laughed and waved his hand. "Mistakes happen, especially at airports," he said. "Besides, if you hadn't taken my bag, I would never have met you." Then he invited them to join the family dinner that evening, and Faisal's father happily accepted. At dinner, Amir, who was the same age as Faisal, held the compass as if it were treasure.

A week later, Faisal and his father were back at the airport, ready to fly home. Faisal had made a new friend, tried spicy noodles he could hardly finish, and promised Amir he would send messages every week. When he lifted his suitcase onto the belt, his father noticed something tied to the handle. It was a bright yellow ribbon. Faisal shrugged and grinned: "Some lessons you only need to learn once."

pages.text: Most mornings, the mountains near Abha disappear into the clouds, but this Friday was different. It was the day of the Asir Junior Cycling Race, and fourteen-year-old Yousef had been training for it for six months. He checked his old blue bike one more time. It had belonged to his uncle Khalid, who had won the same race twenty years ago.

At the starting line, Yousef had butterflies in his stomach. Next to him stood Tariq, the boy who had beaten him in every race last year. "Nice bike," Tariq said with a smile that wasn't very friendly. "Did you find it in a museum?" Yousef didn't answer. He just tightened his helmet and stared at the road ahead.

When the whistle blew, thirty riders rushed forward. The first part of the course went steeply uphill, and Yousef's legs were soon burning. Then he remembered his uncle's advice: "Don't race the others on the hill. Race the hill." He kept a steady pace, and slowly he passed one rider, then another, until only Tariq was ahead of him.

Near the top, the fog rolled in so quickly that Yousef could barely see his own front wheel. The air turned cold and wet, and the road became slippery. Then, through the grey cloud, he heard a crash and a cry of pain. He found Tariq lying beside the road, holding his ankle, with his bike upside down a few metres away.

"Go on," Tariq said through his teeth. "This is your chance to win." The finish line was only three kilometres away, and nobody else was in sight. For a moment, Yousef imagined the gold medal around his neck. Then he got off his bike and knelt beside his rival.

Tariq's ankle was badly twisted, and his chain had come off. Yousef had watched his uncle repair bikes a hundred times, so he fixed the chain in less than two minutes. "Can you ride if you keep your weight on your good foot?" he asked. Tariq nodded, surprised. "Why are you helping me?" he asked quietly.

"Because nobody should be alone in this fog," Yousef replied. They rode down the mountain side by side, slowly and carefully, while Yousef called out every bend in the road. Behind them, other riders were catching up fast. Just before the finish line, two boys flew past, and Yousef and Tariq crossed the line in third and fourth place.

Yousef didn't get the gold medal, but something unexpected happened at the ceremony. A marshal standing in the fog had seen everything, so the organiser gave Yousef a special award for sportsmanship. The crowd cheered even louder than they had for the winner. Later, Tariq limped over with a real smile and said, "Next year, I'll beat you fair and square." Yousef shook his hand and laughed, "We'll see."

pages.text: For three months, Yousef had spent every evening in his grandfather's garage in Yanbu, building a robot. It was the size of a small suitcase, with four wide wheels for the sand and a long arm that could pick up plastic bottles. He called it Sahm, which means 'arrow' in Arabic, because it always went straight to its target. On Thursday, Sahm would compete in the national school science competition in Jeddah.

On Monday afternoon, Yousef took Sahm to the beach for a final test. At first, everything worked perfectly: the robot collected bottles, bags and an old flip-flop, and dropped them neatly into its box. Then, suddenly, it stopped, turned around and rolled towards the dark rocks at the end of the beach. 'Sahm, come back!' Yousef shouted, but the robot ignored every command.

Yousef carried it home and checked every wire, but he couldn't find anything wrong. The next evening, the same thing happened, and this time Sahm beeped loudly and refused to move until Yousef switched it off. 'It's broken,' he told his grandfather, sitting on the garage step with his head in his hands. 'After all that work, I'm back to square one.'

His grandfather, who had been a fisherman for forty years, listened quietly and poured him a cup of tea. 'When my boat's engine made a strange noise, I didn't always fix it immediately,' he said. 'Sometimes I listened first, because the noise was trying to tell me something.' Then he asked what sensors the robot had, and Yousef explained that Sahm could detect heat and small movements in the sand.

That night, they went back to the beach with a torch and let Sahm go wherever it wanted. It led them straight to the rocks and stopped beside a small hole in the sand, where something was moving. Yousef knelt down and held his breath as a tiny sea turtle pushed its way out, followed by another, and then dozens more. 'They're hatching,' his grandfather whispered. 'Your robot found a nest.'

But something was wrong: instead of crawling towards the sea, the baby turtles were heading towards the bright lights of the road behind the beach. 'They're confused,' said his grandfather. 'They follow the brightest light, because they think it's the moon shining on the water.' Yousef thought fast, switched on the powerful lamp on Sahm's head and drove the robot slowly down to the water's edge, and one by one, the little turtles turned and followed the light into the waves.

By the time the last turtle had disappeared into the sea, it was nearly midnight. Yousef had recorded everything on his phone, but he had missed two evenings of practice, and Sahm still wasn't perfect at collecting rubbish. On Thursday in Jeddah, the other robots were faster and smarter, and Yousef didn't win first prize. However, when he showed the judges his video, the whole hall went silent, and then everyone began to clap.

A week later, a letter arrived from a marine research centre on the Red Sea coast. The scientists wanted to borrow Sahm to find turtle nests and guide the babies safely to the sea, and they invited Yousef to help them program it. 'You see?' said his grandfather with a smile. 'Your arrow didn't miss its target. It just found a better one.'

pages.text: Faisal stared at the empty page on his laptop. His history teacher, Mr. Hamdan, had asked everyone to write about "a journey from the past", and the deadline was only a week away. "Everyone's going to write about the same famous travellers," he complained to his grandfather over a glass of mint tea. Grandfather smiled, put down his glass and said, "Then perhaps you should write about one that nobody knows."

Grandfather disappeared into his room and came back with a small, rusty tin box. Inside was a faded photograph of a steam train standing at a station, and next to it lay a brass whistle on a leather string. "This is Madinah, more than a hundred years ago," Grandfather explained. "The boy in the corner of the photo is my grandfather, Saleh. That whistle saved a train full of people."

Faisal leaned closer as Grandfather told the story. The Hejaz Railway had opened only a few months earlier, and pilgrims could now travel from Damascus to Madinah in days instead of weeks. Saleh was twelve, and every morning he walked along the tracks outside the city, collecting firewood for his family. One spring night in 1909, a terrible storm hit the hills, and by morning the rain had turned a dry valley into a rushing river.

"When Saleh reached the small bridge, his heart sank," Grandfather said quietly. "The water had washed away the ground under the rails, and they were hanging in the air like a broken ladder." Far in the distance, Saleh could already see black smoke rising, which meant the morning train was coming. Without thinking twice, he pulled off his red headscarf, climbed onto a rock and waved it above his head as hard as he could.

"The driver saw him just in time, and the train stopped only a few metres from the bridge," Grandfather continued. "Afterwards, the driver took this whistle from his own neck and gave it to Saleh to thank him." Faisal turned the whistle over and noticed tiny letters carved into the metal. "It's a wonderful story," he said, "but how can I prove it's true? My teacher will want evidence."

The next day, they visited the Hejaz Railway Museum in the old station building in Madinah. Faisal showed the whistle to the guide, a young woman named Ms. Noura, who examined it carefully. "These letters are the driver's initials," she said, her eyes widening. "Wait here. I think we have his logbook in our archive."

Twenty minutes later, she returned with a thick book whose pages had turned yellow with age. She opened it to a page from April 1909 and read the driver's words aloud: "Train stopped near the broken bridge. A brave local boy, Saleh, warned us. Without him, we would all have been lost." Faisal felt goosebumps on his arms, and when he looked up, he saw tears shining in his grandfather's eyes.

A week later, Faisal presented his project, and the whole class stayed silent until the very end. Mr. Hamdan gave him top marks, but the best moment came a month later, when the museum asked to borrow the whistle. Now it sits in a glass case beside the old photograph, with a small card that reads: "Saleh's Whistle: the boy who saved the train." Every time Faisal visits, he remembers that history isn't only about famous people; sometimes it's about a boy, a red scarf and one moment of courage.

pages.text: Yousef had always thought that the Farasan Islands were the quietest place on Earth. Every summer he stayed with his grandfather, Jaddi Salem, who had been a fisherman for forty years and knew the sea better than his own house. "The sea talks," Jaddi Salem liked to say, "but only to people who are patient enough to listen." Yousef usually laughed, because the only thing he ever heard was the wind.

One evening, while they were walking along the shore, his grandfather suddenly stopped and pointed at the sand. A wide track, like the marks of a small tractor, led from the water up to the dunes. "A green turtle came here about two months ago to lay her eggs," he whispered. "If I'm right, her babies will hatch very soon, maybe even tonight."

Yousef couldn't believe his luck. He had seen turtles in documentaries, but he had never imagined he would watch real ones come out of the sand. They sat at a safe distance and waited as the sky turned from orange to deep purple. Then Yousef noticed something that worried him. Further along the beach, a large family had set up a camp with bright lamps, a barbecue and loud music.

"That's a problem," said Jaddi Salem, frowning. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the light of the moon on the water. If they see stronger lights on land, they get confused and crawl in the wrong direction." At that moment, the sand began to move, as if it were breathing. One tiny head appeared, then another, then dozens more.

To Yousef's horror, the hatchlings turned away from the waves and started heading straight towards the camp. Some of them were already being chased by a hungry ghost crab. "We have to do something now, or they won't survive until morning," Yousef said. His heart was pounding, but he ran towards the lamps before he could change his mind.

A tall man in a white thobe looked up in surprise as Yousef arrived, out of breath. "Excuse me, sir," Yousef said politely, "could you please switch off your lamps for a few minutes? There are baby turtles on the beach, and your lights are pulling them away from the sea." For a second, the man looked annoyed, but then his young daughter shouted, "Baba, look! They're coming this way!"

Within seconds, every lamp was turned off and the music stopped. In the sudden darkness, the silver moonlight returned to the water, and the little turtles slowly changed direction. Yousef and the family's children walked beside them, carefully keeping the crabs away without touching the babies. One by one, the hatchlings reached the wet sand and disappeared into the waves.

Later, the family insisted that Yousef and his grandfather join them for tea and dates. "My father taught me to respect the sea," the man said, "but tonight your grandson taught me something new." Jaddi Salem put his hand on Yousef's shoulder and smiled. "You see?" he said quietly. "The sea talks, and tonight you finally listened."

pages.text: Two days before Eid, Grandma Noura slipped on the kitchen floor and hurt her wrist. The doctor said she had to rest it for three weeks, which meant no cooking at all. Every year, the whole family gathered at her house for her famous chicken kabsa, and nobody had ever made it except her. "Who will cook it this time?" asked Reem, who was thirteen and secretly loved being in the kitchen.

Grandma smiled and pointed to an old notebook on the shelf. "Everything you need is in there," she said. But when Reem opened it, her heart sank. Someone had spilled tea on the kabsa page years ago, and the amounts of the spices had become brown smudges that nobody could read.

Her younger brother, Saud, offered to help, although he had never cooked anything more difficult than an omelette. "How hard can it be?" he said, chopping onions with tears running down his face. He turned the heat up high to save time, and within minutes the kitchen was full of smoke. The onions were black, and they had to start again from the beginning.

By evening, they had finished their first attempt, and they were feeling rather proud of themselves. Then their father tasted it and tried very hard to keep a straight face. "It's... interesting," he said politely, reaching for a glass of water. Reem took a spoonful and almost choked, because they had added far too much salt and almost no spices at all.

That night, Reem couldn't sleep, so she sat in the quiet kitchen and closed her eyes. She tried to remember standing next to Grandma when she was small, watching the big pot bubble. Slowly, the smells came back to her: warm cinnamon, sweet cardamom, and something sharp and smoky that she couldn't name. Suddenly she remembered Grandma breaking small dark balls into the pot and letting her smell them first.

In the morning, she searched the cupboards until she found a jar of dried black limes, called loomi. "That's it!" she shouted, so loudly that Saud dropped his breakfast. This time, they cooked the onions slowly until they were golden, and they tasted the sauce again and again before adding anything else. Little by little, they got the hang of it, and the kitchen began to smell exactly like Eid.

On the first day of Eid, aunts, uncles and cousins filled the house, and Reem felt butterflies in her stomach. She and Saud carried the huge tray of rice and chicken into the majlis and placed it in front of Grandma. Everyone went quiet as Grandma took her first bite with her good hand. She chewed slowly, said nothing for a long moment, and then her eyes filled with tears.

"This tastes just like my mother's kabsa," she said softly, and the whole room cheered. Later, Reem admitted that she had never been able to read the smudged page. Grandma laughed and said, "Neither could I, habibti. I stopped using that book forty years ago, because the real recipe was always in my nose and my heart." Then she placed the old notebook in Reem's hands and told her it was hers to keep, and to fill with her own recipes one day.

pages.text: Faisal had always thought his grandfather's old cassette player was just a piece of junk. Then one evening in Jeddah, while he was helping to clean the storeroom, he found a dusty box of tapes labelled in faded handwriting. One of them said "The Sea Songs, 1975." When Faisal asked what it meant, his grandfather went quiet for a long moment.

"Before oil changed everything, my father was a pearl diver," Grandpa Saleh explained. "The men used to sing on the boats to keep their rhythm while they pulled the heavy ropes. Each boat had a singer called the nahham, and his voice could be heard across the water." He smiled sadly. "I recorded my father singing when he was old, but I've forgotten most of the words, and I haven't listened to that tape for years."

Faisal's school was planning a Heritage Day, and every class had to present something from the past. Faisal had an idea: what if his class could bring the sea songs back to life? His friends Omar and Yousef were excited, but there was a problem. When they played the tape, it twisted and snapped after only twenty seconds.

Faisal refused to give up. He carefully repaired the broken tape, the way he had seen in an online video, and copied the recording onto his laptop. The sound was crackly, and some words were impossible to understand. Still, he could hear a deep, powerful voice, waves in the background, and dozens of men clapping in perfect time.

For two weeks, the boys practised every afternoon. Omar, who was good at drumming, played the rhythm on a small drum borrowed from the school, while the others clapped and answered the singer's lines. Yousef searched the library and discovered an old book about pearl diving that contained some of the missing words. Gradually, the song began to sound less like a lesson and more like a real conversation between a leader and his crew.

On the morning of Heritage Day, Faisal felt as if his stomach was full of butterflies. The hall was packed with families, and his grandfather was sitting in the front row, leaning on his walking stick. Faisal had planned to sing the leader's part himself, but suddenly his voice felt tiny. "If I make a mistake in front of Grandpa," he whispered to Omar, "I'll never forgive myself."

Omar began the drumbeat, and the class started clapping slowly, like oars hitting the water. Faisal took a deep breath and sang the first line, his voice shaking at first but growing stronger. Then, near the end, he reached a line that nobody had been able to find, and he froze. In the silence, a deep, rough voice rose from the front row and finished the line perfectly.

Grandpa Saleh was on his feet, singing words he hadn't sung for fifty years. The boys answered him, the audience began to clap along, and for a moment the whole hall seemed to rock like a boat on the waves. Afterwards, with tears in his eyes, Grandpa told Faisal that hearing the song had brought the missing words back to him. "You didn't just fix a tape," he said, hugging his grandson. "You gave me back my father's voice."

pages.text: Lina was thirteen, and she had read every detective novel in her school library at least twice. She always carried a small blue notebook, just in case a real mystery ever came her way. That Friday, the whole family had gathered at her grandmother's house in Taif. Before the noon prayer, Grandmother took off her gold ring, placed it on the bathroom windowsill and washed for prayer. Twenty minutes later, when she returned, the ring had disappeared.

Soon everyone was searching under the carpets and behind the cushions, but the ring was nowhere to be found. Aunt Huda crossed her arms and looked towards the kitchen. "Maryam only started working here last month," she said quietly. "Nobody else was near that bathroom." Maryam's face went pale, and Lina noticed that her hands were shaking. "We shouldn't jump to conclusions," Lina said firmly. "A good detective needs evidence first."

Lina went straight to the bathroom and examined the scene carefully. The window had been left wide open, and the sill was covered in a thin layer of dust from the garden. There were no fingerprints in the dust, only some tiny scratches, as if something small had walked across it. Next to the scratches lay a single brown feather. Lina photographed everything and wrote down the details in her notebook.

Next, Lina interviewed her mother, who had been cooking lunch. "Maryam was with me in the kitchen the whole time," her mother said. "She was cutting vegetables, and she never left the room." That gave Maryam an alibi, but it didn't explain where the ring had gone. Lina chewed her pencil and frowned. Someone, or something, had taken it.

Then her little brother Saud came running in with a complaint of his own. "Somebody stole my silver key ring last week!" he said. "I left it on the balcony, and it just vanished." Grandfather laughed and said, "Things have been going missing all month, and those noisy birds in the palm tree have been driving me crazy." Suddenly, Lina's eyes lit up, because she remembered reading that some birds love to collect shiny objects.

To test her theory, Lina set a trap. She folded a piece of shiny silver paper, placed it on the windowsill and hid behind the curtain with her phone ready. For a long time, nothing happened, and her legs began to ache. Then a brown bird with a bright yellow beak landed on the sill, picked up the paper and flew off towards the tall palm tree. "Got you!" Lina whispered, and she had recorded the whole thing.

Uncle Khalid fetched a ladder and climbed carefully up the palm tree while everyone watched from below. "There are no eggs, so I won't disturb any chicks," he called down. A moment later, he gave a loud shout of surprise. Inside the untidy nest were Saud's key ring, two bottle caps, the silver paper and, shining in the middle of it all, Grandmother's gold ring.

Aunt Huda turned to Maryam and said, "I'm truly sorry, I judged you without any reason." Maryam smiled and accepted her apology, and Grandmother hugged Lina tightly. "From now on, you are the official detective of this family," she announced, and everyone laughed. That evening, Lina opened her notebook and wrote two final lines: "Case closed. Look for the truth, not for someone to blame."

pages.text: Faisal had read every superhero comic in his school library, so he knew exactly what a superpower should look like. When his own power finally arrived, on an ordinary Tuesday in Jeddah, it was nothing like the comics. He knocked a glass of mango juice off the kitchen table, and suddenly the whole world stopped. The glass hung in the air, the clock on the wall went silent, and his mother froze in the middle of a sentence.

Over the next week, Faisal tested his power as carefully as a scientist. He discovered three rules. He could stop time only once a day, it lasted exactly three seconds, and while everything else was frozen, he could only move as slowly as he normally did. Three seconds wasn't even long enough to catch the glass of juice, which had landed on his foot.

"So you can't fly, you can't lift cars, and you can't run fast," his best friend Omar said, trying not to laugh. "Your superpower is basically a very long blink." Faisal had told nobody else, and now he was beginning to wish he hadn't told Omar either. He had tried to use his power to score a goal in football, but by the time he had taken two steps, time had started again and the goalkeeper had caught the ball. "Real heroes have real powers," he said sadly.

That weekend, Faisal helped his grandfather in his small spice shop in Al-Balad, the old part of the city. The narrow street sloped down towards the main road, and men pushed heavy carts full of boxes up and down it all day. His grandfather noticed that Faisal looked unhappy. "In my experience," the old man said, weighing a bag of cardamom, "the people who make a difference aren't always the strongest ones. They're the ones who pay attention." Faisal nodded politely, but he didn't really understand.

In the afternoon, his little cousin Yousef came to visit and immediately ran outside to chase a cat. At the top of the street, a delivery man had left his cart for a moment, and it was loaded with wooden boxes of dates. Without warning, the cart began to roll. It picked up speed as it rattled down the hill, heading straight for Yousef, who hadn't noticed anything.

Faisal stopped time without even thinking about it. Everything went silent, and he knew he had only three seconds, so he couldn't possibly reach Yousef or push the heavy cart away. Instead of panicking, he did what his grandfather had said: he paid attention. He noticed a thick rope hanging from the cart, and he saw that its end was lying right next to an iron ring on the wall of the shop. With his last second, he stepped forward and dropped the rope through the ring.

Time started again with a crash of noise. The rope pulled tight, the cart jerked to a stop just a metre from Yousef, and two boxes fell off and broke open, spilling dates all over the street. Yousef stared at the cart, then at the cat, then burst into tears. The delivery man ran down the hill, apologising again and again, and people came out of their shops to see what had happened. Nobody could explain how the rope had got through the ring.

Later, while they were picking up dates together, his grandfather looked at Faisal with a curious smile. "Quick thinking," was all he said, but Faisal had a feeling the old man understood more than he showed. That night, Faisal began drawing his own comic, about a hero called Captain Three Seconds. On the first page, Omar asked the captain what anyone could possibly do with just three seconds, and Faisal wrote the answer in big letters: "Enough, if you use them wisely."

pages.text: Every winter, Faisal's family drove into the desert north of Hail for three days of camping. This year, thirteen-year-old Faisal had brought a power bank, two games and a new map app on his phone. "Who needs the stars when you have satellites?" he joked, while his grandfather put up the tent. Grandpa Saleh only smiled and poured the cardamom coffee.

That first night, Grandpa pointed at the sky above the dunes. "That small, steady star is Al-Jadi, and it always sits in the north," he said. "Our grandfathers crossed this desert by following it." Faisal nodded politely, but he was secretly checking his phone. His sister Lama, who was eleven, listened to every word.

The next afternoon, their father asked them to collect dry wood for the fire and warned them to come back before sunset. Faisal promised, sure that his app would guide them home. They walked from dune to dune, picking up branches and following the tracks of a desert fox, and they didn't notice how far they had gone.

When the sun disappeared, the sand turned grey and every dune looked the same. Faisal took out his phone, but the screen flashed once and went black. "The battery's dead, and I left the power bank in the car," he whispered. Lama grabbed his arm. "We're lost in the middle of nowhere!"

For a moment, Faisal felt panic rising in his chest. Then he remembered Grandpa's calm voice. "Keep calm," he told Lama, and himself. "We walked north all afternoon, so now we need to go south." They looked up at the sky, which was slowly filling with thousands of stars.

"There it is," Lama said, pointing. "Small and steady, just like Grandpa said." Faisal turned so that Al-Jadi was behind him, and they began walking with the star at their backs, even though the wind was cold and the branches felt heavier with every step.

After nearly an hour, Faisal noticed a faint orange light far ahead. Then a smell reached them on the wind: wood smoke and cardamom. "That's our fire!" Lama shouted, and they ran the last part, sliding down the soft sand. Their father was already hurrying towards them with a torch, looking worried and relieved at the same time.

Later, wrapped in blankets beside the fire, Faisal handed Grandpa the wood they had carried all that way. "I owe you an apology," he said. "Satellites are useful, but the stars never run out of battery." Grandpa laughed and poured him a cup of coffee. "Tomorrow night," he said, "I'll teach you three more."

In the end, I decided to join football.

other
second

2-4.q: Your friend asks: "So which club did you choose?" Choose the best reply.
options: In the end, I decided to choose coding because I want to make games.
In the end, I decide coding because games.
I'm torn, so I choose yesterday.
I'm torn among staying and leaving.
I torn between staying and leaving.
I'm torn between staying and leaving.

Next time, I'll make sure to check my answers.

options: Next time, I'll make sure leaving earlier.
I wish I have left earlier.
Next time, I'll make sure to leave earlier.
I wish I had told the truth.
I wish I have told the truth.
I wish I told had the truth.

If everyone planted a tree, we could fight pollution.

3-0.q: One thing our school could do ___ plant more trees in the playground.
options: are
is

options: Yes, I brushed my teeth yesterday.
No, trees are very tall.

to bring

3-1.q: Choose the best reply: "What are you looking forward to about the 2034 World Cup?"
options: I'm really looking forward to seeing the new stadiums.
I'm really looking forward to see the new stadiums.
Yes, I am a football.
It will gives Saudi fans chance to meet people.
It will give Saudi fans the chance meeting people.

Apparently

options: That must be true because it's too far.

What I admire most is the way she listens.

3-3.q: He has achieved his dream by ___ every day.

practised

To do this job, you need to be creative.

options: then

To sum up, sport brings people together.

options: Other point

options: To sum up, thank you.
First of all, yes.
